units: a covered market is in poor condition
the roof lets the water through
the sellers are short of space
the aisles are clogged with shoppers
inspectors have declared the place unhealthy
a group of sellers puts forward a three-part answer
the requests concern the roof, the aisles and the drainage
a local body has approved the idea but lacks money
the works would be done in the quiet season
the sellers hope the buyers will come back
text: Nothing about the old market hall keeps the weather out any longer. Its timbers have rotted, cracked panes let the rain drip onto the stalls below, and the concrete floor turns slippery the moment the damp rises. Traders grumble about cramped pitches that press one against the next, while shoppers shuffle down an aisle packed tight. A traders' group has now put forward a plan in three parts. It asks first for the roof to be relaid, then for wider central walkways, and finally for drainage that would clean up premises the inspectors called unfit. The district council backed the idea and is hunting for the money. Work would begin out of season, so that no trader loses a day's selling. The traders will put up with the mess, sure that a repaired hall will win back the custom that had been drifting away.

units: two public spaces are set side by side
one is old and the other recent
trees surround the older one
you can stay there without spending
the new space is bright but has no shade
the noise there puts off anyone who would stay
the old one was made for the pause and the recent one for movement
the writer holds that a place is judged by those who stay in it for no reason
text: People set the old square against the recent forecourt as though one belonged to the past and the other to whatever is coming. The comparison is worth taking up again, and more slowly. Ringed by close-planted trees, the old square invites you to sit down and buy nothing at all: an idle man dozes on a bench, children tear about, a stallholder nods off behind her tray. The recent forecourt gleams with pale paving and hard-edged benches, yet it throws no shade at all, and its clatter drives off anyone minded to linger there. One was drawn for the quiet halt, the other for the crossing. We too readily judge a shared space by its polish; it is judged instead by how many people stay in it for no reason. A good place is not the one you walk through but the one you inhabit briefly, then leave with regret.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a mediator works in one particular district
her work falls into four strands
she handles quarrels between neighbours
she receives the two sides in a neutral place
she helps people with their official paperwork
she runs meetings and trains volunteers
she records the closed files meticulously
her colleagues praise her warmth and her helpfulness
she studied social law before taking the post
text: Four strands make up the work of the mediator posted to the northern district, within limits laid down by a written protocol. The first covers quarrels between neighbours: she takes the complaint, checks whether it can be heard at all, then calls both sides to a room that belongs to neither. The second deals with entitlements; she helps fill in the forms and points people towards the right office. The third is prevention, since she runs meetings for whole blocks of flats and trains volunteers. The fourth concerns record-keeping, a task she handles fastidiously, because every closed file must be coded. Colleagues describe her as warm with the public and obliging towards junior staff. She read social law before taking up the post, and rounded that off with a course in attentive listening.

units: a development scheme is judged phase by phase
the consultation of local people was thorough
the papers and the objections were made public
an option that kept a courtyard was turned down without explanation
the building work moved quickly
the signs put up hindered the oldest residents
the finished result looks sturdy and easy to read
the final judgement is divided
the writer would like the opening method taken up elsewhere
text: Following this development scheme stage by stage is the surest way of weighing what it is worth. The opening phase, an open consultation of those living nearby, was handled with real care: minutes went out, objections were written down, deadlines held. The second stretch disappoints, for the client set aside, without adequate reason, the variant that would have kept the inner courtyard. Then came the building work, pushed through at a speed that deserves credit, though the signs put up around it confused the oldest residents. The handover, last of all, shows a plain scheme whose materials look hard-wearing and whose routes are easy to read. The verdict is therefore mixed: an exemplary method at the start, a murky ruling in the middle, a creditable end. One would want the next operation to keep the first quality without repeating the second failing.

units: the writer has just moved somewhere else
the building looked sound in the pictures
the shared parts turned out to be damaged
the lack of upkeep had discouraged the occupants
that discouragement made the decay worse
the writer called a meeting of the neighbours
few people came for want of notice
those present shared out the cleaning and wrote to the landlord
the state of the building has improved since
the writer asks for news from the person written to
text: I am writing from the flat I have just moved into, and I think you will grasp my mood soon enough. The building looked perfectly sound in the pictures I was sent; on the day I arrived I found a battered stairwell, letterboxes prised open and an entryphone that made no sound at all. Since nobody was looking after the shared parts, the tenants had long given up trying, and that giving-up had let the decay spread further still. So I called a meeting. Word went round badly and few people turned up, but there were still enough of us to settle on two things. We split the cleaning floor by floor, and we wrote jointly to the landlord. The stair light works now, the front door shuts properly, and the neighbours say hello. Tell me how your own move went, because I would like to set it beside mine.

units: vehicles take up the pavement of the street
people have to walk on the road used by cars
the writer says one can act without waiting for the authorities
the residents logged the blocked stretches for a week
they took pictures and wrote a short note
a local committee has to comment on a scheme without cars
two bollards were put in at a street corner
the roads department promised to paint lines
the writer sums up the method in three moves
text: You are asking what has gone wrong in our street, so here it is, straight out and unvarnished. The trouble is that the whole pavement gets used for parking, which means we push the prams along the road with the traffic instead. The next question answers itself: can we do anything without waiting for a ruling from above? We can, and we have started. For a week we logged every blocked stretch, we took photographs of it, we wrote a short note. Then you will say, who ever reads a note like that? The district committee does, as it happens, since it has to comment before the walking scheme goes to study. The upshot: two bollards went in on the corner, and the roads team promised paint on the ground before long. It has not worked everywhere, fair enough, but the method holds. Watch, measure, ask in writing.

units: a volunteer compares two districts outside a community centre
in the lower district people come in person
in the upper district they ring instead of travelling
the manager puts the gap down to the distance
a woman using the service describes a packed waiting room below
the same room above is almost empty
the number of staff differs between the two places
the volunteer finds the comparison incomplete without that fact
the speakers agree on the part played by available staff
text: Asked outside the door of the community centre, a volunteer weighs up the two districts that she knows well. Down here, she says, people knock on the door for a form; up on the hill they ring first and rarely make the journey. The man in charge softens that: to his mind the gap comes from the distance, not from the character of the people. An older woman using the service joins in and insists that the waiting room down here is packed from opening time, whereas the one up the hill struck her as nearly empty. He accepts the difference and puts it down to staffing: two workers below, only one above. The volunteer concludes that the comparison would be quite unfair if that detail were left out. All of them settle on one point: what gets done depends less on the district than on the number of hands.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: farming communities managed their own water
that management covered several matters
the upkeep of the water point fell to every household
the basin was cleaned and leaks were watched for
the sharing followed an order of turns that was respected
that order decided whether the crops succeeded
a gathering of elders punished those who broke the rule
the punishment took away a watering turn
these rules were passed on by word of mouth
they lasted as long as the mutual dependence did
text: Long before water ever ran from a tap, farming villages arranged it themselves, and the arrangement reached into several separate matters. There was the spring first of all, whose upkeep fell on every household alike: the basin was scoured, the stones reset, seepage watched for carefully. There was next the sharing, governed by turns that nobody dared disturb, since the order of watering decided what the harvest would come to. There was last the penalty, handed down by a gathering of the oldest men, which stripped the offending household of its coming turn at the water. None of this was written; it passed from use to use and lived in the memory of neighbours. What strikes you, looking back from a distance, is how long it held: as long, exactly, as the mutual need that had brought it into being.

units: a shared budget runs through ordered stages
the residents first hand in their proposals
every proposal follows the same form
technical officers then judge what can be built
requests that cost too much or fall outside the scope are dropped
the proposals kept are priced and then grouped by area
the vote is held at scattered reception points
the projects placed highest go into the works programme
progress is made public at regular intervals
the procedure comes round again from one year to the next
text: A shared-budget scheme runs through a fixed sequence, and it can be set out here step by step. The first stretch opens the door to ideas: every resident writes a proposal on one standard form, with a short description and a precise location. Technical officers then look at whether each submission can be built; they throw out anything that belongs to another budget or goes over the ceiling that has been agreed. Next comes the appraisal, where the surviving proposals are priced and then grouped by area. Voting follows over a short spell, at reception points spread right across the whole patch. The proposals that come out top are written into the works programme, and a progress table goes up at every stage. This calendar comes round again the following year, with nothing much altered in it.

units: a lift broke down in a block of flats
two occupants were stuck between two floors
one of them was elderly and the other very young
the repair was slow in coming
neighbours talked to them and brought them something to drink
a resident chased the firm responsible by telephone
the two occupants were freed during the night
the residents then drew up a list of contacts
they demanded stricter servicing
the manager agreed to change the worn cables
text: It took no more than a broken lift for the building to learn what it had never known about itself. The car came to a halt one evening of heavy rain, between two floors, carrying an elderly tenant and a teenage boy. Repair was slow in coming, so the wait stretched out, and word of it travelled from landing to landing. One neighbour went down to talk through the door, another brought a bottle of water down, a third rang the maintenance firm again and again. What followed was not merely the release of the two occupants, late that night, from the stalled car. Because they had at last spoken to one another, the residents drew up a list of contacts the week after, and then demanded stricter servicing. The manager, blamed in writing for the state of things, agreed to have the worn cables replaced.
